visible.summary: Fiji is workable for trans visitors — the Pacific islands' leader. Same-sex relations decriminalised in 2010; the 2013 Constitution bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity AND expression — reportedly the only constitution in the world with that explicit pairing. Counterweights: no gender-marker change mechanism, and the Asia Pacific Transgender Network documents high rates of violence and harassment against trans people. Suva has an organised community (Haus of Khameleon, Rainbow Pride Foundation).
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2010 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
visible.localsOnly: No gender-marker change mechanism — resident-facing; the APTN-documented violence and harassment rates describe residents' experience.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Constitutional protection vs documented street violence gap.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex conduct decriminalised 2010 (Crimes Act); Fiji among the first countries to ban SOGI discrimination constitutionally — SO protection in the 1997 Constitution, reinstated and expanded to gender identity and expression in the 2013 Constitution; workplace SO protections since 2007; health professionals barred from trying to change sexual orientation. Traditional third-gender vaka sa lewa lewa recognised culturally but no legal gender recognition route; no same-sex marriage/civil unions (Marriage Act 2002: one man, one woman); intersex bodily autonomy unprotected. At a glance: same-sex relations illegal per overview flag, LGR No, orgs cannot register.

Asia Pacific Alliance policy brief and case study, 'Legal Gender Recognition in Fiji' (2023): the 2013 Constitution's discrimination protection on gender identity and expression is described as unique worldwide, yet legislative/policy frameworks permit NO gender-marker change and do not recognise traditional third-gender identities — headline constitutional protection with zero implementation for trans people, resulting in documented marginalisation and discrimination.

Human Rights Watch (11 Apr 2005): two men (one an Australian tourist) received two-year prison sentences under colonial-era Penal Code Art 175 (up to 14 years) for consensual sex; HRW urged charges dropped and release, citing Fiji's 1997 constitutional ban on SO discrimination (Fiji one of first two countries worldwide, with South Africa); the judge called the acts 'so disgusting... any decent person vomit'. Documents the enforcement era before the 2006 no-arrest policy and 2010 decriminalisation.

PinkNews (10 Jul 2006): the Fijian High Commissioner confirmed an official policy that men engaging in consensual gay sex will no longer be arrested — the practical end of enforcement two years before the Crimes Act 2010 decriminalisation; NZ AIDS Foundation (Exec Dir Rachael Le Mesurier) linked criminalisation to undergrounding of sex and HIV spread.

GlobalGayz country page (pre-2013, undated): Fiji timeline — 1997 second country in the world to enshrine SO non-discrimination; 2006 no-arrest policy confirmed; 2007 state of emergency ousted PM; 2009 Constitution abolished; 1 Feb 2010 full decriminalisation under Crimes Act 2010; Marriage Act 2002 bars same-sex marriage; ~322-island archipelago. Legacy-era overview — its claim that SOGI discrimination was not banned predates the 2013 Constitution.

Sydney Morning Herald (14 Apr 2005): PM Laisenia Qarase rejected international pressure to legalise gay sex, calling homosexuality a sin in 'the conservative Christian nation', days after an Australian tourist and a Fijian man received two-year sentences — the political/religious climate context behind the sodomy-law enforcement that HRW protested.

visible.summary:
Samoa is workable for trans visitors — anchored by one of the world's most institutionalized third-gender traditions. Fa'afafine (and fa'atama) are culturally embedded: recognized as heirs to customary land and eligible for matai (chiefly) titles within fa'a Sāmoa, organized nationally through the Samoa Fa'afafine Association (a formal UN UPR stakeholder since 1987), and visible through a famous pageant culture. Samoa repealed its colonial-era “female impersonation” crime in 2013, so no law touches gender expression itself.

The remaining negatives are modest for a visitor: no anti-discrimination law and no legal gender recognition (both resident-facing); documented discrimination, cyberbullying and gender-based violence against fa'afafine (APTN peer-led study — primarily resident/domestic contexts); isolated police-harassment reports (2 respondents, no convictions); and village fono councils that enforce conservative dress and behaviour norms. The unenforced sodomy statute is a situational risk for a fraction of visitors, not a trans-universal one.
visible.tangentialFactors: The unenforced sodomy statute is a situational risk for visitors travelling with partners, not a trans-universal one.
visible.localsOnly: The APTN-documented discrimination, cyberbullying and gender-based violence against fa'afafine occur primarily in resident/domestic contexts; village fono norms govern resident life.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Fa’afafine cultural embedding is informal protection; criminalisation unenforced.

sources.claim: APTN (9 May 2024): Nadi, Fiji convening gathered gender-diverse community members from Samoa, Cook Islands, Vanuatu, Kiribati, Fiji, Tonga, West Papua, PNG — documents the Pacific MVPFAFF+ spectrum (fa'afafine in Samoa and American Samoa, fakaleiti in Tonga, fakafifine in Niue, etc.) as living community infrastructure Samoa participates in.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Samoa's criminalisation of same-sex activity (up to 5 years under the Crimes Act 2013).

Samoa Fa'afafine Association (SFA) stakeholder report for Samoa's UPR (39th session, 2021): 'The Protection of the Rights of Fa'afafine/Fa'atama/LGBTIQ/SOGIESC persons in Samoa' - describes the culturally unique third-gender identities fa'afafine and fa'atama and documents lived experiences and struggles, with the aim of establishing grounds for non-discriminatory policy and legislation.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters feature covers Samoa's third gender (fa'afafine) delicately balancing sex and religion.
NOTE: The APTN Samoa socio-economic study returned no extractable text at fetch time (image-based PDF).

RNZ Pacific (3 May 2013): Samoa's new Crimes Act, in force that week, scrapped the crime of impersonating a woman — Samoa Fa'afafine Association president To'oto'oali'i Roger Stanley expressed relief; interview also confirms the community was not then agitating to repeal sodomy provisions, i.e. decriminalisation outcome on that front remained unchanged.

Schmidt, 'Redefining Fa'afafine: Western Discourses and the Construction of Transgenderism in Samoa' (Intersections, Aug 2001): fa'afafine = 'in the manner of a woman'; academic analysis argues fa'afafine identities are both viewed through and reshaped by Western sexuality/transgenderism discourses, with Auckland's Samoan diaspora as a contact zone — background for how visitors may encounter the term.

UN Free & Equal Pacific information sheet (Aug 2015): FAQ on sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status in the Pacific - documents the fa'afafine of Samoa (with American Samoa and Tokelau) among the diverse pre-colonial Pacific gender identities that are 'important parts of the cultural treasure of the region'.

visible.summary: Kiribati is dangerous for trans visitors. Male same-sex conduct criminalised (14 years, unenforced); no LGR; tiny, isolated, church-dominated society with no visible community infrastructure.
visible.tangentialFactors: Male same-sex conduct criminalised (14 years, unenforced) — formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners.

sources.claim: 76crimes reprint of 2015 US State Department report, Kiribati section: consensual sex between men illegal, 5–14 years' imprisonment depending on offence, no prosecutions reported; constitution bars discrimination by race/national origin/colour (observed) with land ownership restricted to I-Kiribati; gender discrimination prohibited only in employment and poorly enforced; no SOGI non-discrimination law and no reported societal discrimination or violence.

University of Hawai'i at Manoa research guide 'Gender Identity and Sexual Identity in the Pacific and Hawai'i': resources on sexual and gender diversity across the Pacific, documenting identity expressions defined as homosexual/transgender only in Western vocabulary — including the Pinapinaaine/Binabinaaine role of Tuvalu and Kiribati (Besnier 2014, 'Gender on the edge', p. 327).

76crimes (7 Aug 2015): at the 21st-session UPR, France, Slovenia and Chile urged tiny island nation Kiribati to decriminalise homosexuality — the Kiribati delegation made no response, but said it is considering Uruguay's advice to adopt legislation prohibiting discrimination covering gender, sexual identity and sexual orientation.

76crimes (21 Nov 2016): the UN General Assembly rejected the amendment to defund the SOGI Independent Expert mandate, 84–77; the article notes Sri Lanka and Kiribati as two countries that at the time still had anti-homosexuality laws — dated criminal-law status evidence for Kiribati.

visible.summary: Solomon Islands is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct criminalised (14 years); no LGR; documented social hostility; weak state capacity post-Tensions; no open community infrastructure.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalised (14 years, unenforced) — formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners.

sources.claim: ILGA World Database jurisdiction page for Solomon Islands: documents the legal status — same-sex conduct criminalised under colonial-era law, up to 14 years.

US State Department 2013 Human Rights Report for Solomon Islands: no security-force abuses; violence and discrimination against women prevalent; the LGBT section notes criminalisation under the penal code but no prosecutions.
US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Solomon Islands: documents lengthy pretrial detention, corruption, violence against women - general context; no LGBT-specific abuses reported.
US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Solomon Islands: documents the RAMSI assistance mission, the Lusibaea case, and general human-rights conditions - baseline assessment.

SIBC (8 Jun 2018): Governor General Sir Frank Kabui used his Queen's Birthday address to warn that 'same sex marriage cannot populate the world' — a dated official statement of elite hostility to recognition; no same-sex marriage law exists and Parliament has not legislated one.

Human Dignity Trust profile: Solomon Islands criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, maximum penalty 14 years' imprisonment (Penal Code provisions); the profile documents the colonial-law basis and the absence of recorded prosecutions in recent years.

Wikipedia reference summary: male and female same-sex sexual activity is illegal and punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment, but the law is not enforced; LGBTQ people face legal challenges not experienced by other residents, with no relationship recognition or non-discrimination shield.

visible.summary: Nauru demands real caution. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 2016; tiny population (~12,000); no LGR; no documented anti-trans violence; the asylum-detention legacy shaped its international image but not its LGBT law. Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2016 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.

sources.claim: US Mission Geneva (Mar 2011): publishes the full text of the Joint statement on ending acts of violence based on sexual orientation & gender identity, delivered by Colombia on behalf of 84 countries — Nauru is among the signatories (with Fiji, Marshall Islands, Micronesia and others). For this record: dated evidence of Nauru's diplomatic position supporting SOGI rights.

Human Truth Foundation 'LGBT Rights Across the World' (Vexen Crabtree, 2025): the Vexen LGBT Equality Index ranks Nauru 101st at -0.10, far below top-ranked Germany/Spain at 4.88 and below most Pacific neighbours. For this record: a comparative-index placement for Nauru.

The Guardian (29 May 2016), headline-level (article body did not survive retrieval — nav shell only): 'Nauru decriminalises homosexuality and suicide' — the 1899 Queensland-derived criminal code provisions repealed, replacing them including attempted-suicide provisions. For this record: the dated decriminalisation event.

Kaleidoscope Trust Nauru country page: Nauru decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in 2016 but same-sex marriages and unions remain illegal; intersex and transgender people have no explicit legal recognition or protection, and no employment-discrimination protection for LBTI people; Nauru supported the 2011 UN HRC Joint Statement, and its last CEDAW state report (2016) contained no LBTI-specific information. For this record: the current legal-status snapshot for trans/intersex people specifically.

visible.summary: Palau demands real caution. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 2014; small, US-associated, tourism-dependent; no LGR; no documented anti-trans violence. Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2014 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.

sources.claim: US Mission Geneva (22 Mar 2011): Palau is among the 84 countries on whose behalf Colombia delivered the joint Human Rights Council statement calling for an end to violence and human-rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity — early dated diplomatic signal of Palau's position.

Erasing 76crimes (16 Oct 2014): Palau decriminalised homosexuality — per Human Dignity Trust, Palau's Attorney General confirmed the new Penal Code (signed by the President in April 2014) dropped the sodomy offence formerly at s.2803 Ch.28 'Sex Crimes' Title 17 (up to 10 years' imprisonment); at its 2011 UPR Palau had accepted recommendations to repeal criminalisation and combat LGBT discrimination; the move dropped the global anti-sodomy country count to 79.

Scoop/OHCHR Pacific piece (c. 2011): lists Palau among 70+ Pacific/global jurisdictions with laws criminalising same-sex relations still on the books, and records that Palau and Nauru accepted recommendations to decriminalise homosexual acts during their Human Rights Council UPR appearances — documenting Palau's stated commitment to repeal.
